summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France. French law governs matters of justice and civil status, so gender recognition, criminal procedure and the anti-discrimination framework that a trans visitor encounters are set by Paris, while the territorial institutions in Papeete administer daily life, health policy and policing resources.

Detention follows the gender marked on an identity document, and Article D248 of the French Code of criminal procedure requires separate men's and women's establishments. A trans woman holding a male marker is therefore held with men. BuzzFeed News, reporting on the situation in France in January 2018, treated this as a legal grey area rather than a settled outcome. France's Law 2016-1547 removed the requirement of medical transition or surgery for a legal change of civil-status gender, but no norms were added on how to house detainees accordingly. The CGLPL, the national preventive mechanism for places of deprivation of liberty, concluded in an opinion of 25 May 2021 that serious violations against transgender detainees persist across French detention, a treatment that reaches the prisons of French Polynesia.

France's Penal Code has carried gender identity as a protected ground since 18 November 2016, when it replaced the earlier wording of sexual identity in article 225-1, and in 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by imprisonment. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks during 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. Assaults motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract heavier penalties.

The conversion-therapy ban passed the French Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022. The Académie Nationale de Médecine has described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an epidemic-like phenomenon and a primarily social problem, and a March 2024 report commissioned from The Little Mermaid Observatory called gender-affirming care a health scandal and youth transness a social contagion. A bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, with no National Assembly action recorded since 23 July 2024. Late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2.

Access to transition-related care inside French Polynesia is constrained by limited local expertise. Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua's government tabled a social-security Bill to fully reimburse hormonal treatment, progesterone and testosterone, on the same basis as mainland France, but after heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the Bill failed to gain sufficient support. Some trans people, referred to locally as raerae, encounter family rejection and move to mainland France for specialised services.

The social environment is markedly more open than the legislative record suggests. The mahu is a traditional Polynesian social role in which a person embodies both male and female qualities and holds cultural standing, and mahu and rae-rae are visible in daily life across the 118 islands. OutTraveler, writing on 4 July 2025, described inclusivity as ingrained enough that Pride displays are absent, with a visiting couple reporting mainstream acceptance and no Pride flags.

Partner recognition follows the French civil-status framework: civil solidarity pacts date from 1999, same-sex marriage passed the National Assembly 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, and assisted reproduction was extended to lesbian couples from September 2021. Since March 2019 French higher education institutions are expected to use trans students' preferred names, a provision that governs the territorial university in Papeete as well.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between social climate and legal machinery is the central tension for a trans visitor. Out Adventures presents Tahiti and Bora Bora across the 118 islands as a relaxed, gay-welcoming South Pacific culture, and OutTraveler reports acceptance without Pride displays, yet both assessments are travel-oriented and neither records a trans-specific finding for French Polynesia. Visible cultural presence of mahu and rae-rae does not by itself indicate how police, prosecutors or prison authorities will treat a trans traveller whose documents or presentation conflict.

France's punitive-hate-speech machinery also sits above the territory. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, punishable by up to €45,000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment; it was criticised by Reporters Without Borders and defended by the Chirac government, and Christian Vanneste was convicted under it in January 2006 before that conviction was cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Sexual orientation became a protected ground in employment and services in 1985, and the Labour Code covers sexual orientation and gender identity in recruitment and training.

Attitudinal data relevant to the wider French framework is uneven. In 2014 only about 20% of overseas residents viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77% in metropolitan France, and Mayotte, another overseas collectivity, reports frequent family rejection and discrimination. Le Refuge estimated that 3-4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy.

Schools observe 17 May under the 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign and enrolment forms use parent 1 and parent 2, an environment that shapes how families and young people in French Polynesia encounter gender diversity. A comparison worth holding: some trans residents relocate rather than seek care locally, which is a materially different strategy from the one available to a short-term visitor who must be treated where they are.
localsOnly:
Residents of French Polynesia live under the territorial institutions in Papeete for health, social security and education policy, which is why the failure of the reimbursement Bill before the Territorial Assembly translated directly into out-of-pocket hormone costs for people who cannot wait for a Paris-level decision. Care remains concentrated in mainland France, and families rejecting a gender-diverse relative can force relocation rather than resolution.

The mahu carries recognised cultural standing within Polynesian society, and rae-rae participate openly in community life across the islands, a local vocabulary that differs from the minority-identity framing of French law. Residents can invoke the national protections directly: gender identity under article 225-1 of the Penal Code since 2016, transphobia as an aggravating circumstance since 2017, and the conversion-therapy ban in force since 1 February 2022, with reporting routes through territorial police.

For trans students at the territorial university, the expectation that higher education institutions use preferred names has applied since March 2019. Residents also sit under the same civil-status route to legal gender change created by Law 2016-1547, which no longer requires medical transition or surgery, though the housing and placement consequences of that change in detention remain unsettled.

Political advocacy is conducted through the Territorial Assembly and through dialogue between churches and the University of French Polynesia, as recorded in RNZ Pacific's coverage, so care-access reform is pursued territorially rather than being a settled entitlement.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 has been applied to, or cited in, any specific inspection of a prison in French Polynesia is not sourced here; the inventory establishes only that the French framework is applicable in the territory's prisons. The BuzzFeed News treatment of Article D248 as a legal grey area is a characterisation made in January 2018 and no later French court ruling resolving it is present in the inventory.

Whether the Senate bill banning medical transition under 18 advanced after 23 July 2024 is unresolved, as is the current status of the March 2024 compensation bill for men arrested under the repealed 1960 indecent-exposure clause, for which the Senate had not voted as of the inventory.

Several items in the source coverage concern France nationally with no stated bearing on French Polynesia and should be read as background rather than territorial findings: the repeal of sodomy provisions by the Penal Code of 1791 and the silence retained by the Penal Code of 1810; the indecent-exposure clause of article 330, second alinea, inserted in 1960 by the Mirguet amendment and repealed in 1980; the statute of 6 August 1942 setting consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 in 1982; and the internment of LGBTQ people in Alsace and Lorraine after 1940. The conversion-therapy helpline estimate and the 2014 overseas-versus-metropolitan attitude figures derive from mainland or aggregated French data, and the Mayotte findings concern a different overseas collectivity.

The inventory contains no entry, visa or border-screening rules specific to trans travellers, no data on documentation changes at Papeete's airport, and no trans-specific violence statistics recorded inside French Polynesia itself. The Out Adventures source carries no trans-specific finding and was excluded on that basis. The hostile language attributed to the Académie Nationale de Médecine and to the commissioned March 2024 report is documented as French debate and no source in the inventory shows territorial officials adopting it.
